newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Russia platinum stock could run out soon - JM.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia platinum stock could run out soon - JM.

text.p: Russia's stocks of the rare precious metals platinum could run out within a year, according to an official of the world's largest refiner of these metals Johnson Matthey Plc.
And the country's stocks of palladium could be depleted early in the next century.
Russia is the largest exporter of palladium and the second largest supplier of platinum after South Africa.

But its major production facility Norilsk Nickel cannot produce enough to meet export demand, and so for years the export agencies have been dipping into government-held stockpiles to meet the market's needs.
The size of the stockpiles is a tightly held government secret but they are believed to be declining.

"Platinum stocks have contracted but nobody knows by how much. However, there is probably not more than a year's supply left in stock," said Jeremy Coombes, Johnson Matthey's general manager, marketing of the precious metals division.
"Palladium is longer but with the palladium market growing so strongly they will contract," Coombes said.
"More is being used for electronics and auto catalysts and that is going to mean Russia keeps dipping into the stockpile.
"We anticipate the end of stocks by the first couple of years of the next century."
Russia's platinum and palladium stocks have probably been run down by about one million and five million ounces respectively over the past two years, Johnson Matthey estimated.
Last year alone, two million ounces of palladium were exported from reserves.

A long term issue for users of the metals is that current prices -- around $390 per ounce for platinum and $170 for palladium -- there is little profit left for the South African miners to plough back into expanding output.

"They have been helped by the rand depreciation but that is a short-term profit because it is absorbed by cost inflation," said Keith Green, director of marketing for Johnson Matthey's precious metals division.
The officials were interviewed by Reuters ahead of the release on Monday of the company's Platinum 1997 annual review of the markets for platinum group metals (PGMs).
The survey shows balanced markets last year and forecasts few fireworks in 1997.
Platinum demand rose only 40,000 ounces in 1996 to 4.88 million ounces while supply fell 90,000 ounces to 4.9 million.
"Platinum demand was flat in 1996 and the market was in balance until early this year," said Coombes.
"1997 will be the same sort of year as 1996," he added.
Platinum and palladium are used in electronics and chemical applications and are the key elements in the auto catalysts that neutralise noxious gases in car exhausts.
Platinum is also popular as jewellery, especially in Japan, and palladium is widely used in dental alloys.
Demand growth for both metals has climbed on increasingly strict air pollution legislation and on the rise of the electronics industry.

But in 1996 car makers cut platinum use for the second year in succession -- to 1.82 million ounces, compared with 1.85 million in 1995 -- and it could be a few years before demand in the sector picks up significantly.
"Demand was up in Latin America and South East Asia, but in North America there has been a switch from platinum- and palladium-based auto catalysts," Coombes said.

European car makers are expected to use 10 percent more PGMs this year, even if their car production is up only one percent. But that too will be due partially to a switch to cheaper palladium, which needs more metal per car.
Further tightening of environmental legislation by 2000 will mean bigger catalysts using more platinum, Coombes added.
Use of platinum by the jewellery fabricators increased marginally by 40,000 ounces to 1.85 million ounces last year as increasing sales in the U.S. and China offset a flat market in Japan.

Demand from car makers anxious to cut costs helped boost palladium use by 30,000 ounces in 1996 to 6.15 million ounces, but demand from the electronics sector fell by 560,000 ounces to 2.06 million ounces.
The auto industry used 2.31 million ounces versus 1.80 million ounces in 1995.
Record sales of the metal from Russia (4.6 million ounces) and South Africa (1.69 million ounces) increased supply by 480,000 ounces to 6.82 million ounces.
Johnson Matthey forecast prices of the two metals to remain around current levels this year.
Platinum was expected to hold a $360-$400 per ounce range and palladium $130-$160, but questions on Russian exports meant that "significant excursions above and below this range" were forecast.
